title: Cell enlargement, polarity competition and migration persistence
subtitle: Size-dependent polarity responses and prospective cellular measurements
stage: Size, polarity response and heading persistence
overview: Working hypothesis: WGD-associated enlargement changes how established polarity is organized and replaced; these changes may provide a physical basis for greater migration persistence. The theoretical contribution tests size under unchanged local kinetic parameters. Length differs between model cells to represent WGD-associated enlargement, rather than elongation during a turn. Existing migration observations supply empirical motivation; new paired WGD motility results retain a substantial, explicitly reserved contribution.

Figure 2 separates size-dependent initiation and cue-width responses from temporal class signatures: initiation-limited resetting, saturating activation with visible gap retention, and pulse-2 progress after loss of visible activity. The full Holmes width series shows finite replacement at all tested lengths for sufficiently broad cues; narrow-cue censoring cannot establish a growing penalty.

Cue placement separates sliding of the incumbent from takeover by a new region; enlargement slows both routes. Weak boundary susceptibility changes differently across models: terminal response at the largest size is 70% of the smallest-size response in Wave-pinning, 9% in Goryachev, 91% in Holmes and 99% in Spring. The deterministic boundary response predicts physical domain drift without fitting when shared translation is retained. Wave-pinning’s C60/C20 drift ratio at f = 0.001 is 0.494 predicted and 0.473 measured. Holmes and Spring show much weaker susceptibility changes. The independent-edge approximation is refuted by boundary co-motion; Goryachev’s drift prediction remains quantitatively inconsistent and does not explain its full heading persistence.

Enlargement extends heading memory and raises noise tolerance, while the size advantage weakens as input strengthens. The weak-input drift in Wave-pinning, Holmes and Spring is close to quadratic in input, connecting Figure 4 to the deterministic edge-response test in Figure 3. Direct event accounting distinguishes persistent secondary onsets from certifiable no-parent births. Certified takeover probability declines with size in each model at a common finite follow-up, but different certification fractions and pooled inputs limit population inference. Per-perimeter birth direction varies by model; it is not a universal consequence of enlargement. At native moment amplitude, eligible weak-input heading loss is allocated almost entirely to domain motion. As secondary domains appear, membership changes and the amplitude/shape/background remainder can grow; the pattern varies with model and size. This exact accounting remains descriptive, and the original unit-normalized point-region artefact is retained as a supplementary diagnostic.

The prospective pilot table fixes model-linked cellular observables before the SUM-159 data arrive. Directions are conditional hypotheses; unavailable model measurements remain unavailable. Activity heading, observed migration summaries and conditional OU velocity-memory estimates remain separate evidence.

This is a working manuscript outline. Figures 1 and 5 and the reserved Figure 6 experimental section retain their preceding content. Activity polarity, modelled replacement, observed migration and conditional OU velocity memory remain distinct readouts; their biological connection is an experimental hypothesis.

sections.title: Figure 1. Enlargement changes the cue duration required for lasting polarity replacement
sections.role: Comparative theoretical foundation: five established models, three finite challenges, and two distinct scalar replacement gates.

assets.caption: Current canonical comparison, 10 October Spearman revision; corrected independent-endpoint deBelly.
assets.page_title: Figure 1. Five models and three finite challenges

legend: A, Example wave-pinning preparation from a homogeneous state using a finite left patch. The cue ends at 0.773 native time units, whereas the subsequent basal relaxation establishes the polarized profile later (reported establishment arrival about 116). Coloured profiles and orientation samples distinguish input duration from autonomous development. The grey late interval is verification, not additional stimulation. Profiles are scaled for display.

B, Three rightward finite challenges restart the identical qualifying nominal-amplitude, relative-20% basal checkpoint at each model and length: fixed physical support 3 (Spring 0.2 native length units), relative support 20%, and a linear ramp with constant physical slope. Patch peaks remain fixed within each model; a fixed-slope ramp has a larger peak in a longer domain. Goryachev patches use the independently selected, length-independent multiplier K=64 (peak 6.4), which makes this a response-permissive comparison rather than a calibrated equal biochemical dose across models.

C, Spearman rank correlation between length and the shortest tested passing pulse duration, separately for orientation replacement and strength replacement, across Wave-pinning, Goryachev, corrected deBelly, Holmes 3 and Spring. Each cell reports the correlation and included successful-length count. All audited scalar successes enter, including those failing the separate native-field tail criterion. At least four distinct successful lengths and nonconstant durations are required; censored and preparation-ineligible cases receive no invented time. The companion duration curves retain all lengths and field-status markers.

After each positive pulse, input returns to the native basal value for 10,000 native time units. Orientation requires all 201 final-500 samples to have scalar orientation above 0.05 and contrast at least 0.05, with orientation range below 0.005. Strength additionally requires every tail orientation to be within 1% of the absolute initial leftward scalar orientation; it does not compare individual pole heights or amounts. The separate native-field tail flag requires pointwise range and projected 500-unit drift within 0.1% of frozen field scales. The reported duration excludes preparation and recovery. It is the shortest passing tested duration, with sampled fail/pass boundaries refined to 1%; narrower unobserved intervals are not excluded.

deBelly uses independently commanded corrected endpoints, rather than the deprecated in-loop centered extension. Spring length and time retain native units and are not silently converted to micrometres or seconds. Model-specific axes and stimulus definitions prevent interpreting cross-model amplitudes or clocks as biologically calibrated equivalents.
narrative: Fixed-width and relative-width patches show perfectly increasing rank order among observed successes in Wave-pinning, Goryachev, Holmes 3 and Spring; enlargement often increases the finite stimulation required for a retained response.

The response depends on the cue geometry and model. Spring has a negative constant-slope association (Spearman correlation -0.874 for both gates), while Holmes orientation under the constant-slope cue is nearly unassociated with length (0.047).
Corrected deBelly curves are nonmonotone despite moderate positive rank correlations. The full duration curves and eligibility ranges are essential to the result.
These are deterministic polarity-replacement experiments. They motivate, but do not measure, spontaneous polarity memory or migration persistence.
measurements: Mechanism-linked cellular follow-up would match local input support, amplitude and duration, track the original and challenged activity regions through stimulation and withdrawal, and distinguish orientation replacement from recovered activity strength. This validation is proposed and has no experimental results in this outline.
limitations: Correlations are conditional on observed scalar success, rather than an unbiased summary of all possible sizes or a universal scaling law. Ineligible starts are distinct from responses unobserved by the finite horizon.

A retained scalar response can coexist with a changing native field. Only 13 of the 72 corrected deBelly scalar successes pass the separate native-field tail flag. Resolution checks from the earlier centered-deBelly campaign cannot qualify the corrected replacement thresholds.

sections.title: Figure 2. Replacement resistance in enlarged cells has distinct size and pulse-memory signatures
sections.role: Separate size-dependent initiation and cue-width responses from observable pulse-memory classes.

assets.caption: Figure 2. Revised size and pulse-memory signatures.

legend: Enlarged cells resist replacement through distinct initiation, cue-width and pulse-memory signatures.
A, Incumbent excess amount, extent and peak, normalized to each model’s reference, across 97 retained states.

B, Initiation is the time from cue onset until maximum in-cue activity minus the profile minimum exceeds 10% of the model’s L19 incumbent excess peak. Area 1, width 3.8; times are normalized to L19. All six deBelly upper bounds are 0.5 native units (downward arrows); first-update sampling leaves its size dependence unresolved.

C, Replacement time (first eligible challenger share ≥ 0.75) versus length, with a line per width and rows for areas 0.5, 1 and 2. Upward triangles/arrows are lower bounds: the cue never replaced within the horizon (6,000 Wave-pinning; 10,000 Goryachev/Holmes; 2,000 deBelly; 100 Spring, native units). Broad cues rescue Holmes across all lengths; narrow-cue censoring does not establish a growing penalty. Spring native widths equal the displayed widths divided by 38.

D, Gap-1 activity kept versus pulse-2 gain as a fraction of headroom (Eq. 1). Four equal pulses, total ON 1.5 times the model-length commitment calibration; gaps 0–16 pulse durations. Holmes L31–39 uses the L27 calibration. Other models are grey; lightness indicates L. Open circles at x = 0 code activity below the existing visibility gate. At the left wall, deBelly/Spring gain on pulse 2 despite no visible activity; Goryachev never does. The deBelly L19/gap16 first-gap endpoint was checked against native fields.

E, L39 gap4 challenger-share histories, labelled kept / lost / lost then commits; shading marks cue ON. deBelly includes full recovery; others show one post-train pulse duration. Continuous raw shares include below-gate values. deBelly’s later timing and fields remain numerically sensitive (supplement).

F, Schematic biosensor predictions for the same pulse train and equal-dose width series in WGD− and enlarged WGD+ cells: delayed rises and resets; saturation with gap retention and strong width rescue; or gap collapse followed by commitment, with weaker width rescue. Predictions are prospective. Model kinetics are unchanged.

equations.description: s₁ and s₂ are challenger shares at pulse ends 1 and 2; s_gap1 is the first-gap-end share. An observed endpoint below the existing visibility gate is coded as zero visible share in D; its raw value remains in the CSV.

narrative: Enlarged cells resist replacement through distinct initiation, cue-width and pulse-memory signatures.
The full width series shows that Holmes can replace at every tested length when the cue is broad enough; narrow-cue censoring cannot establish a growing width-penalty ratio.
Pulse-2 headroom gain separates low visible retention with residual progress from the initiation-limited reset response. Saturating activation retains visible activity through gaps.
measurements: Measure first in-cue biosensor rise, then vary width at fixed integrated dose.
Measure pulse-1, gap-1 and pulse-2 challenger shares under the same pulse train, followed by eventual commitment.
limitations: Commanded input areas and native clocks are not calibrated across models.
deBelly initiation is unresolved within the first native update; later-gap timing and endpoint fields remain numerically sensitive.
D codes known below-gate activity at x=0; the exact raw ratio remains in the plotted-value CSV.
Holmes large-length trains have no target-length commitment calibration; visible retention differs from eventual replacement.
The three classes describe selected deterministic regimes; WGD biosensor predictions are prospective.

sections.title: Figure 3. Enlargement slows both turning routes and selectively suppresses boundary susceptibility.
legend: A. Wave-pinning activity at C = 30 for a cue straddling the incumbent boundary (i, gap −1) or separated from it (ii, gap 4). Rows show 0%, 50% and 90% of cue-direction heading, then the relaxed cue-free profile. Grey: cue support; diamonds: inter-region saddles; ticks: heading.

B. Half-turn time versus cue-edge gap from the incumbent’s 10%-contrast boundary. Increasing sizes use lighter solid, intermediate dashed and darker dotted curves; chemical C = 30, 37.8, 47.6, Spring 2.5, 3.15, 3.97. Vertical lines mark the first resolved two-region saddle at half-turn; grey bands mark undefined heading at ≥1 size; triangles are time lower bounds. Enlargement slows both turning routes. C–D use different size grids, so these panels do not establish a matched-size relation between strong-cue turning and weak-pulse response.

C. Control-subtracted displacement of the pulsed half-contrast boundary divided by peak input a, at f = 0.001. A Gaussian pulse has SD ℓ = 1.5 and duration τ = 50 (Spring 0.15 and 5); peak a = 10⁻⁴ of the native input reference. Shades denote chemical C = 20–60 or Spring resting C = 1–3. Insets show displacement integrated to 20τ, divided by pulse dose aτ, then normalized to the smallest size on a common 0–1.1 axis. Largest/smallest terminal gains are 0.701 Wave-pinning, 0.914 Holmes, 0.989 Spring and 0.0878 Goryachev. Both edges and half/double amplitudes are checked in the supplement.

D. Above: predicted versus Figure 4 physical tracked drift for f ≤ 0.01. Filled markers retain shared translation; open markers retain the rejected independent-edge candidate. Measured pulse gain sets response amplitude; the unchanged native linearization supplies spatial shape, and the exact input covariance supplies forcing statistics. Nothing is fitted to drift. Below: predicted versus measured Dₛ(C)/Dₛ(Cmin) at the same f, removing the dominant input-strength scaling. Wave-pinning at f = 0.001 gives C60/C20 = 0.49 predicted and 0.47 measured. Lines: 1:1; bars: whole-seed-bootstrap 95% CI. Goryachev C20/C30 at f = 0.01 have no polarized mean-state boundary; the normalized prediction at that f also lacks its C20 reference.

Wave-pinning, Holmes and Spring have shared-translation prediction/observation medians 1.021, 1.080 and 1.069. Resolved quarter-window edge correlations are 0.980, 0.983 and 0.997 in the two exemplar seeds, refuting edge independence. Goryachev retains large quantitative disagreement. Tracked drift is conditional on trackable domains and is distinct from total heading decay.

Two cellular assays follow: vary photoactivation offset from straddling to separated placement and measure half-turn time; separately apply a weak brief boundary pulse and track both boundaries through withdrawal. The second assay measures susceptibility and common translation; it does not uniquely assign Figure 2 mechanism classes. Native units are not calibrated across models.
sections.role: Size-dependent susceptibility links deterministic boundary perturbation to weak-input domain drift; cue position separates two slower turning routes in enlarged rings.
narrative: Cue placement separates sliding of the incumbent from takeover by a new region; enlargement slows both routes. Weak boundary susceptibility changes differently across models: terminal response at the largest size is 70% of the smallest-size response in Wave-pinning, 9% in Goryachev, 91% in Holmes and 99% in Spring.

The deterministic boundary response predicts physical domain drift without fitting when shared translation is retained. Wave-pinning’s C60/C20 drift ratio at f = 0.001 is 0.494 predicted and 0.473 measured. Holmes and Spring show much weaker susceptibility changes. The independent-edge approximation is refuted by boundary co-motion; Goryachev’s drift prediction remains quantitatively inconsistent and does not explain its full heading persistence.
measurements: Vary photoactivation offset from straddling to separated placement; measure time to half-turn.

Apply a weak brief pulse across the leading-edge boundary; measure both boundary displacements, common translation and covariance. This readout complements rather than uniquely identifies the Figure 2 mechanism classes.
limitations: Panel B and C–D use different size grids and perturbation strengths; a matched-size comparison is not established. One pulse does not identify spatial response shape; native linearization supplies that explicit assumption, while measured pulse gain supplies amplitude. Two float16 exemplar seeds support the covariance check, with short-lag precision limits. Goryachev’s unresolved mean-state boundaries and quantitative drift disagreement remain visible. Physical domain drift is not total heading decay or empirical cell migration persistence.

Measured terminal displacement per pulse dose supplies amplitude; the unchanged native response supplies spatial shape. The covariance derivation is in the methods and supplement.

sections.title: Figure 4. Enlargement extends heading memory as fluctuating input changes domain dynamics
sections.role: Size-dependent heading persistence, edge drift and secondary-domain competition under fluctuating input.
legend: A. Drifting peaks, same-rate null relocations and perimeter-rate null relocations give size exponents 2, 0 and −1. Null kymograph widths follow circumference; time increases upward. Autocorrelations C(ℓ) use solid C20 and dotted C60 curves. The null relocations are illustrative whole-peak moves, distinct from measured dominant-region replacements and birth-to-takeover events.

B. Larger rings retain heading across stronger fluctuating input. Input fraction f sets the ensemble mean to f times the native reference (Wave-pinning 0.1; Holmes 1; Spring 4; Goryachev 6.4). Input is positive lognormal, mean × exp(σZ−σ²/2), with unit-variance Gaussian driving field Z and σ=1. The spatial parameter ℓ and OU correlation time τ are 1.5 and 50 in chemical models; Spring uses basal-physical ℓ=0.15 and τ=5, with physical ℓ scaling with its changing circumference. Local size exponents α and noise-tolerance folds use model hues and light-to-dark circumference ramps. Open symbols in the exponent and drift panels identify conditions flagged as forced by the frozen matched-mean/lower-noise controls; open diamonds in the fold panel identify Goryachev irrespective of forcing; vertical intervals are pointwise 95% whole-history bootstrap intervals. Boundary triangles retain off-scale values. 125/260 local neighborhoods resolve, including 11 Goryachev neighborhoods. Largest-size tolerance folds are Wave-pinning 2.373, Holmes 2.155, Spring 3.088 and Goryachev 4.122. f₁/₂ is the first input crossing of C(ℓ)=0.5 at reference lag 2000 (Spring 200); Spring circumference is multiplied by 20 only in the fold panel.

C. Matched small- and large-ring kymographs are centred on their initial activity heading to the nearest spatial bin. Time increases upward; black outside ticks mark persistent dominant-region replacements. Activity scales are shared within Wave-pinning, Holmes and Spring; Goryachev uses 0–9.2 at C20 and 0–83 at C60. Ensemble C(ℓ) curves are below. A low-contrast initial heading may have weak biological meaning despite a defined numerical centre.

D. Physical within-tenure drift Dₛ is normalized by the smallest size at the same input. Unity gives the equal-physical-drift geometric expectation α=2. Weak-input log–log fits for f≤0.01 give exponents Wave-pinning 1.96–1.99; Holmes 1.94–1.95; Spring 1.87–1.93. The second row shows the existing event-based predicted/observed decay only where f≤0.01 and multiple regions occupy at most 5% of frames. 45/47 eligible point comparisons lie within 15% (Wave-pinning 16/16; Holmes 15/16; Spring 14/14; Goryachev 0/1). These point predictions assign the scored-event mean angular loss to unscored replacements; this remains an assumption. Goryachev uses separate logarithmic ordinate ranges: 10⁻⁷–2 for normalized drift and 0.003–3.3 for decay ratio; other models use 0.2–8 and 0.3–3.3. The actual mean circumference, C̄, enters physical-to-angular conversion. Figure 3D independently predicts this measured drift from deterministic edge responses.

E. i, Certified no-parent secondary births per actual perimeter-time: new tracks persist at least five frames, have a preceding incumbent, and have conservative support enclosures disjoint from all previous regions. Rates are lower bounds; discarded masks prevent exact birth/split classification. ii, Observed incidence of five-frame global dominance by 20τ (1000 chemical units; 100 Spring), conditional on certified births with that follow-up. Inputs f>0.01 are pooled. Distance d subtracts estimated incumbent half-width (preceding full-basin amount divided by twice global contrast h) from the shortest centroid arc. Vertical intervals are 95% whole-history bootstrap intervals. A lower finite-horizon incidence can reflect delayed or less frequent takeover; lifetime success remains unidentified. Figure 2B–C motivates separating initiation from incumbent removal. iii, Native-amplitude-aware signed heading-loss allocation over the condition’s analysis lag. M, shared-region motion; A, coexisting amount; B, track membership including unresolved splits/mergers; R, amplitude/shape/background remainder. Point-region Shapley changes are scaled by mean native endpoint moment amplitude, so pure rigid translation gives M=1, R=0. Components sum exactly to observed heading loss but are descriptive, convention-dependent shares. The symmetric-log color scale is linear within ±0.05 and spans ±1; dots indicate values outside ±1, gray unavailable pairs. The unit-normalized point-region diagnostic and its normalization artefact are preserved in the supplement; eligibility and equations are detailed in Methods.

equations.description: Q is the normalized point-region moment; P=M₁/M₀ is measured from the native field. Its amplitude r prevents the unit-modulus single-region normalization artefact.

equations.math: \Delta P_j=\bar r\,\Delta Q_j\ (j=\mathrm{M,A,B}),\qquad\Delta P_{\mathrm{R}}=\Delta P-\bar r\,\Delta Q
equations.description: The three ΔQ components use the symmetric Shapley convention for motion, coexisting amount and membership; r̄ is mean endpoint native amplitude. R closes the native moment change and includes amplitude variation, shape and background. This is an accounting convention, not causal attribution.
Pooled signed fractions are sums of L_j divided by total measured heading loss. They retain cancellation, can exceed one, and depend on the stated accounting convention; they are not causal shares.
C(ℓ) is activity-heading autocorrelation; C̄ is actual mean circumference. Endpoint eligibility uses |P|≥0.1. Drift closure is shown only at f≤0.01 and multiple-region fraction≤0.05.

measurements: Measure lateral-edge fluctuations, secondary-protrusion births per actual perimeter-time, finite-horizon takeover probability and leading-edge displacement after boundary-straddling photoactivation. Preserve separate WGD-associated cell-size, observed migration and simulated polarity-heading readouts.
limitations: Exact no-overlap birth counts and split counts cannot be recovered for the full campaign because compact records discard native masks/parent IDs. Lower/upper birth bounds and conditional takeovers are reported instead. The global-contrast plateau estimate is not a recovered per-region plateau.

Native clocks are not calibrated between models. A takeover is five-frame global dominance within 20 noise correlation times, not a lifetime success probability. Full-history right censoring, short-followup exclusions and per-condition counts are retained in CSV. Inputs f>0.01 are pooled without reweighting; size cohorts can differ in their event-weighted input composition. A lower incidence by 20τ does not distinguish slower takeover from a lower lifetime probability. A fixed-cohort supplementary incidence curve extends observation to 80τ without extrapolating beyond it.

Heading attribution uses only eligible lag endpoint pairs with measured |P|≥0.1, finite tracked amounts/centroids and all nonzero hybrid totals. Goryachev at f=0.03 has pair coverage 0.666 at C20 but only 0.0109 at C60. Endpoint membership does not reveal events occurring and reversing inside the lag. This algebraic allocation depends on the chosen convention and includes normalized point-region approximation error in its residual.

Historical multiple-front-majority closure point predictions are conditional on scored angles representing unscored replacements: none of 33 point estimates is within 15%, but missing-angle bounds permit agreement within 15% in 24/33 and span unity in 18/33. This cannot generally distinguish omitted heading processes from unscored large-angle replacements. Goryachev’s 37 historical finite point ratios span 0.00575–0.344, with limited dominant-region exposure and angle scoring; missing-angle bounds span unity in 11/37. These diagnostics remain in the supplement and do not motivate the independent exact endpoint allocation.

sections.title: Figure 5. Published migration summaries support a persistence hypothesis with conditional OU interpretation
sections.role: Existing empirical support, with observed migration summaries kept separate from fitted velocity-memory parameters.

assets.caption: Reassembled Figure 5: original A and C–F numerical evidence, revised MSD/curve-shape panel B.
assets.page_title: Figure 5. Migration observations and conditional OU interpretation

assets.caption: Figure 5B continued: enlarged detail with explicit raster-sample caveat.
assets.page_title: Figure 5. Migration observations and conditional OU interpretation

legend: A, Published/digitized enlarged or polyploid-group to reference-group ratios for nine migration summaries, alongside primary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) fit predictions. Xuan contributes sampled mean speed and population mean-squared displacement (MSD) at the last shared lag, approximately 10.95 h; Hosny summaries are group medians. Mallin central-bar statistic is not specified by the source and retains the historical mean approximation. These distinct source summaries are not interchangeable measures of persistence.

B, Upper: twelve chosen display samples from each digitized Xuan population MSD curve (small points) and the unchanged fitted analytical OU expectation (solid lines), on logarithmic lag and MSD axes. These are samples of the published raster curves, not recovered experimental lag positions or independent cell observations; the original experimental lag grid is unknown. The open circle identifies the crossover of the full digitized traces at approximately 2.32 h, computed by linear interpolation in native lag and MSD. The open diamond identifies the different fitted OU crossover at approximately 1.11 h. Lower: descriptive slopes of log(MSD) versus log(lag) fitted in six equal log-lag windows of the full digitized curves (points), and matching-window moving OU slopes (solid lines). Each window spans approximately 0.304 decades; both observed and model slopes use the same full window support. Observed raster columns remain correlated and give no biological sample size or confidence interval. These slopes are newly calculated curve-shape summaries, not author-reported local exponents or fitted OU memory times. A constant power-law exponent would appear horizontal; reference values 1 and 2 indicate diffusive and straight-line scaling. The model does not reproduce the complete observed curvature or the observed crossover. The analytical fit, all fitting targets and numerical inputs to A and C–F are unchanged.

C, Representative Xuan primary-fit model-generated tracks, with sampled speed, total path length and directness (net displacement divided by path length). Both groups use identical spatial scales. The tracks are simulations, not published individual-cell trajectories; a slower sampled trajectory can nevertheless have greater endpoint directness. Dashed chords illustrate the contribution of finite-time displacements.

D, With reference-group parameters fixed, vary enlarged-group persistence and velocity-noise ratios. Separate surfaces show change in the descriptive data-misfit score and in the total regularized objective; the selected fit and equal-group reference are marked. The heuristic score is not a calibrated likelihood, and the surfaces are not confidence regions.

E, Primary paired persistence and velocity-noise estimates for Xuan 2018, Mallin 2023, Jemaà 2017, Jemaà 2023 and the Hosny hypoxic baseline. F, Enlarged/reference persistence folds under the primary 10-minute prior, 5- and 20-minute alternatives and stronger/weaker pooling, with the pooled geometric mean. Priors and pooling define conditional sensitivity scenarios, not uncertainty intervals. The Jemaà comparisons constrain speed alone, leaving persistence/noise tradeoffs dependent on hierarchy and priors.

The fitted population contrasts span stable tetraploids, giant polyploids and treatment-induced polyaneuploid cancer cells (PACCs). The inherited WGD+/WGD− labels in the artwork are comparison shorthand and do not establish matched WGD-only interventions in every study. Hosny observations derive from the recovered preprint; equivalence to the journal version remains unresolved.
narrative: Xuan combines lower sampled speed (0.64-fold) with greater late-lag population MSD (2.08-fold); Mallin combines shorter path length (0.52-fold) with greater directness (3.12-fold). Persistence-related behaviour therefore deserves analysis separately from speed.
Hosny baseline PACCs have greater median path length (1.77-fold) and directness (1.67-fold). Signed migration index is a separate directional summary.

All five primary OU comparisons infer longer velocity memory. The pooled primary persistence fold is about 15.8, and remains above one across the declared prior/pooling scenarios; this is a conditional model result.

The fit does not reproduce the complete Xuan curve shape within its raster envelope, and data-only sensitivity has rank 18 of 22. Optimization completion does not establish model adequacy or uniquely identified persistence times.

The observed Xuan curves cross near 2.32 h while the unchanged fitted OU curves cross near 1.11 h. Matched-window slopes make the remaining curve-shape discrepancy visible; fitted persistence is a conditional summary.
Lower sampled speed can coexist with greater late-lag displacement in the enlarged-group comparison. Its causal connection to polarity mechanisms requires matched activity and migration measurements.
measurements: The new WGD assay should measure matched trajectories directly, with declared sampling and observation duration, and assess speed, displacement, directness and lag-dependent MSD before considering fitted persistence. An activity-polarity memory measurement would complement these quantities without equating activity and velocity.
limitations: Neither these heterogeneous group comparisons nor the OU fits establish that enlargement alone causes persistence. Cell identity, induction/treatment and acquisition differences require explicit treatment in the new experiments.

The requested observed-point/model-line and curve-shape display is implemented. The original experimental lag grid remains unknown; neither display samples nor raster-derived slopes supply independent biological replicates. The observed/model crossover discrepancy remains visible.

supplementary.title: Prospective pilot observables before SUM-159 data
supplementary.role: Specified on 23 October 2026, before SUM-159 WGD+/− motility data; no experimental observations were used.
legend: Prospective directions, not SUM-159 observations or a full statistical preregistration. Freeze sampling, segmentation, physical pulse dose and group inference before comparison; model f and native times have no calibrated cellular equivalents.

Birth rates are model dependent: at f = 0.1, bounds identify a Spring increase and a Goryachev decrease with size. Takeover within 20τ is fixed-horizon incidence; its decline persists through 80τ in the same cohort, while lifetime fate and certification selection remain unresolved.

Common translation tests the drift mechanism. Edge pulses refine susceptibility within routes: Wave-pinning and Holmes share an expansion-constrained class in Figure 2 but predict different edge responses. Combine these readouts with Figure 2 first-rise, width and pulse-gap assays to test initiation-limited reset, saturation/expansion and retained progress after visible activity loss. Activity heading, observed migration and OU-fitted memory remain separate readouts.
narrative: Model drift subset: f ≤ 0.01 and multiple-domain fraction ≤ 0.05. In cells, classify by the observed frequency of coexisting protrusions; model f and native times have no calibrated cellular equivalents.
measurements: Track both lateral half-contrast boundaries of a persistent leading activity/protrusive region. Report their mean-squared physical displacements and cross-correlation over declared lags, including failed single-domain eligibility and changes in region identity. Compare physical displacement before normalizing to perimeter. The two edges are strongly correlated in model exemplars, so report their covariance rather than assuming independence. Report common-mode displacement (left plus right)/2 separately from width fluctuations (right minus left); a single-edge MSD alone cannot distinguish these modes.

With full images retained, call a new connected protrusive/activity region a birth only if it overlaps no region in the preceding frame and persists for at least five consecutive saved frames. Divide by observed perimeter-time exposure; count splits separately. Freeze segmentation, cadence and overlap rules before group comparison.

For each qualifying birth, measure shortest centroid arc distance from the incumbent minus the incumbent half-width, estimated as excess amount divided by twice the declared plateau height. A takeover requires five consecutive frames of dominance. Report right censoring and a common follow-up horizon; distinguish all births from any subset whose identity is certifiable. The revised model comparison uses a common 20-noise-correlation-time follow-up and pools f > 0.01; these conditioning choices must be separated from the cellular analysis. This is fixed-horizon incidence, not a lifetime takeover probability. Record time since birth, cumulative incidence and right censoring. In the same model cohort with at least 80τ follow-up, the decline persists from 20τ to 80τ; finite observation and certification selection still prevent a population lifetime claim.

Define the activity/protrusion vector from the full spatial signal; estimate heading autocorrelation at declared lags with a fixed coherence rule and report excluded pairs. Compare groups at matched analysis lags and observation duration. Keep cell displacement/velocity persistence as a separate observed readout.

Apply a weak, brief photoactivation spot centred on a lateral leading-edge boundary, matched in physical width and duration across ploidy groups. Track both edges through relaxation, subtract a no-pulse control, and check half/double amplitudes. A response supports a mechanism only to the extent that its size trend differs among model predictions. At model f = 0.001, largest/smallest pulse-response gains are 0.701 (Wave-pinning), 0.914 (Holmes), 0.989 (Spring), and 0.0878 (Goryachev); these are native-model size contrasts, not numerical cellular fold predictions. Separately repeat the Figure 3A–B assay with cue placements straddling and separated from the incumbent boundary, measuring half-turn time to distinguish sliding from takeover; the weak local pulse and the finite turning cue are distinct assays.
limitations: No SUM-159 motility data are available in this revision. Directions are prospective and must not be described as confirmed experiments.
Native model times and f are not calibrated to cells. Event holds measured in frames depend on acquisition cadence; select and report that cadence before comparing experimental groups.

The compact model records do not identify every birth, split or local plateau height. Model bounds and certified-subset probabilities do not establish the unconditional cellular birth/takeover directions.

The new observables do not uniquely distinguish the Figure 2 response classes. Weak boundary susceptibility and finite-cue sliding/takeover are different properties; the within-20τ size contrast cannot distinguish slower completion from a change in eventual success.
